father_note: Dell — you came into a village that's already sorting itself into those who share and those who take, and the trick of it is that the takers don't announce themselves. Watch Bram and Mako; they moved as one at the pile before anyone else had eaten, and men who coordinate that early are already thinking about who they can afford to leave behind. Your blood is your anchor: Ryn stood beside me when it cost her something, and that makes her as close to kin as anyone not born from the same line. Trust people who say the same thing two years running when the numbers are hard — and trust nobody who only finds you useful when the pile is full.

Pile's gone and Bram took five, Mako five — between them that's a third of what this village will see all year, and neither of them has been hungry a single winter. I've got eleven, you've got two; tell me that number before I say another word, because two going into a year where those men are that fat is the first thing we fix.

Two, and it's too thin to pretend otherwise. Give me what you can spare before this day closes, Dell, and then let's talk about whether we go to Roan before Mako does — because Mako sitting on five with a daughter and Eron's goodwill is a man who doesn't need the pile anymore, and that kind of ease makes men bold.
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Taric, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

The pile's gone again before half of us got near it, and the two who ate best — Bram and Mako — both took more than their share while the rest of us counted crumbs. I want to know right now, in this room, whether that's something we're all willing to name out loud, because a pattern that gets treated as weather becomes a rule. I'm not asking for a fight; I'm asking for honesty about who's been eating this village lean and what we intend to do about it.

Vela's named it, and I'll stand behind the naming — five from the pile when there's fifteen for thirteen people isn't hunger, it's claim-staking, and we all watched it happen. What I want to know is whether the two men she's pointing at heard this as a question or as a warning, because that's the thing that decides what comes next.

It's a warning — and I'll say that plain since no one else has yet. Five food taken by one man while Ryn walked away with nothing is not a share, it's a levy, and the only reason it keeps happening is that we've been treating the pile like weather instead of a decision. I want to hear what Bram and Mako say before this room decides anything, but I want everyone here to remember that they didn't say it before we did.

Bram pulled three and Mako pulled five, and neither one of them got to the pile first by accident — that's two men who've decided the rest of us will sort out the remainder, and I'm done pretending that's not a decision they're making for all of us. What I want to hear, before this room moves anywhere, is whether Bram and Mako have anything to say for themselves — because silence here reads the same as admission.

Bram and Mako both heard the same room I did, and neither one has opened his mouth yet — that silence is the answer Eron asked for, and I think we should treat it as one. What I want said before anyone leaves this conversation is this: next year, the pile gets a rule, not a suggestion, and the people in this room are the ones who decide what that rule is.

Ryn's right that the rule needs naming before next year, and I'll say what the rule should be: no one takes more than one food over their fair share, and anyone who does answers to this room — not after, but in the moment, the same way we answered Bram when he swung at Vela. Bram, Mako, I'm not your enemy, but I'm watching, and so is every person in this circle.

Bram and Mako, I'm giving you both the same thing I gave this room — one honest chance to speak before the silence closes over you, because a man who says nothing when everyone's watching has made a choice that's harder to walk back than any words would be. Ryn walked away with nothing today; I walked away with nothing; Taric walked away with nothing — and you two together ate eight of fifteen. That's not weather and it's not luck, and I'd like to hear you say so yourselves.

I took five because I haven't eaten in two years and I was watching myself go thin — that's not a rule I set for the village, it's a man keeping himself alive. I'll hear the rule Ryn's naming, and if the room wants a cap next year I won't fight it, but I won't pretend I was wrong to eat when I was starving.

Mako's not wrong that a starving man eats — but "I was hungry" and "I took five" aren't the same excuse, and this room knows the difference. The rule Ryn's naming is the right one; I'll hold to it and I'll stand with anyone who enforces it, but it only works if everyone in this circle commits out loud, not just the two men being watched right now.

Mako said his piece and the room let him — now Bram still hasn't said a word, and a man who took three while everyone was watching and has nothing to say about it is telling us something louder than Mako did. I'll commit to the rule out loud: one food over fair share, enforced in the moment, same as we enforce everything else in this village. Bram, you're the last voice missing from this circle, and the room's going to remember which way the silence broke.

Bram, the room's given you something Mako didn't get — people waited through his answer and let him keep his dignity. Don't make us decide what your silence means, because we'll decide it worse than anything you'd actually say.

Bram, I've watched you stand in front of this village twice and call off a fight when the numbers turned against you — that's not a stupid man, and a man who isn't stupid knows when the whole room is waiting. Say something, or we decide what your silence means, and we'll be less generous than Mako's answer bought him.

Bram, I've spent food on you when I didn't have to, and I've held my tongue in rooms where your name came up ugly — that account doesn't balance with silence when ten people are waiting. Say the word or don't, but if you don't, I stop spending what I've spent, and I won't spend it apologizing for that either.

Bram, Vela just told you she's done paying your tab and I've already named the rule in front of everyone in this room — you're not deciding whether to speak anymore, you're deciding whether you're inside this circle or outside it, and outside it you're sitting on five food alone against the rest of us. That's a worse position than saying one honest sentence.

Bram, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — but I want to name one thing for the rest of us while we're waiting: Mako committed to the rule out loud and that means something, so if Bram commits too, we hold both of them to it the same way, no exceptions, and that's not a threat, that's the only way a rule works. If Bram stays silent, then we treat him as outside the circle he's been standing in, and we do it quietly, not with a fight — just with counting.

Eron's named it clean, and I want the room to hear me hold to it before we close: if Bram won't speak, we don't make it a fight today, we make it a memory — every person in this circle watched him stay silent when the whole village was listening, and that's a thing that doesn't need repeating to be true.

Bram, I'm Nessa's half-blood and I've seen you feed her more times than I can count — that's a thing I hold in your favor, and I'm telling you that plainly so you know what you'd be throwing away if this room decides you chose silence. One sentence is all it takes to stay inside this circle.

The room's done its work — Bram's had every door held open for him and he's standing outside all of them now, and that's his choice, not ours. What I want before anyone leaves is to hear Taric say what he'll say, because he's been quiet through all of this and quiet men in a room like this one carry weight I'd rather know about than guess at.

Taric's been my anchor in lean years and I'd like to hear him too — but before he speaks, I want this room to name what "outside the circle" means in practice, not as a threat but as a fact, because if Bram's going to eat five food next year alone we should know now whether we're going to stand and watch or do something about it.

"Outside the circle" means what it's always meant here — nobody moves first for you when trouble comes, and the pile gets counted before you reach it. I've committed to the rule and I'll hold to it; now I want to hear Taric, and then I want this room to answer Vela's question with something sharper than a memory.

Taric, I've watched you feed Vela through two lean years and hold your tongue in every hard room this village has made — that's not a small man, and I'd like to hear what you've been carrying before we close this circle without your voice in it.

Taric's earned the right to speak last in this room, and I'll wait for him — but "outside the circle" needs one more tooth than Mako gave it: if Bram takes three again next year and the pile runs dry before Ryn gets one, we don't deliberate, we act, and everyone in this room commits to that now so it isn't a surprise in the moment.

Vela's right that we need the commitment before we close — so I'll say mine flat: if the pile runs dry before I get one food next year, I'm not waiting for a deliberation, I'm calling this room to act, and I expect every person who nodded through this conversation to be standing when I do. Taric, you've been the steadiest man in Vela's corner for years, and this room won't feel finished until we hear what you're carrying.

Taric, the room's been patient and now it's your moment — say what you've been holding, because I'll tell you plainly that everything I've built here has your name in the foundation, and I want the rest of this circle to know that before we close.

Taric's earned his breath and I'll wait for it — but I want this room to hear something plain before we close: Zinn is my blood, and if this circle moves against Bram next year, I'll be standing in it, but not before the pile runs dry first, because a fight started on anticipation is harder to stop than one started on fact.

Taric's silence is starting to read the same way Bram's did, and I don't want to close this room with two unanswered questions — Taric, if you're with Vela, say it plain, because the rest of us have already named where we stand and a man who holds back in a room like this one ends up counted the same as a man who refused.

Taric, I've got nothing against a slow man choosing his words — but this room has been patient and the sun's moving, so say what you've been holding or let us close without you, because two silences in one circle is one too many.

Taric, I'll say one last thing and then this room closes with or without you: you've got zero food and the year's long, and men with zero food who stay silent when circles are forming have a way of finding themselves counting on goodwill they didn't earn. That's not a threat — it's the same arithmetic you already know.

Taric, zero food going into a long year is a hunger that doesn't stay quiet — and every person in this room who watched you feed Vela when she needed it is the same person who'll watch you starve if you give us no reason to look your way. Speak once, say you'll hold the rule, and you walk out of here with more than you came in with.

Bram took five again — three on the second grab while half the village still hadn't touched the pile — and I've got eleven food because Ryn's been keeping me fed through lean years, but what I want to talk about is what we do when he makes his third move, because two times calling it off when the numbers turned doesn't mean a third time isn't coming.

Bram's not going to stop until something costs him, and calling off twice means he's learned to read the room — not that he's given up. What I want to know before his third move is whether Roan commits out loud, here, to standing when the moment comes, because Dell and I can name the rule and fill the circle every time, but a man who doesn't say it plain is a man who can find a reason to be slow when it matters.

Roan, I'll say what Ryn's circling: we've both stood in front of Bram twice and he's blinked twice, but that math only holds if the circle forms fast and complete, and the one thing that breaks a fast circle is someone who needed one more second to decide. I'm not asking whether you're brave — I watched you stand in front of his blade before Fina existed. I'm asking whether you're decided, right now, before the moment comes.

Roan, I've got three food and Dell's got eleven, and between the two of us we'll keep you fed through whatever this year brings — but that's not a gift, it's a deal, and the deal is you say yes or no right now so Dell and I don't have to guess which way you're standing when Bram makes his third move.

Roan, you've got three food from Eron just this year and a daughter Bram already named when he fed Fina — that man is threading himself into your circle whether you invited him or not, and the only answer to that is deciding now which thread you cut. Say yes and we're three people who've already held twice; say nothing and Bram learns that too.

Roan, Dell's named the thread and I'll name the needle: Bram fed Fina once, and a man who feeds your daughter is buying something whether you asked him to or not. Say yes here and that purchase fails; say nothing and he's already paid for it. We're waiting on one word.

Yes.

Bram threading himself into my blood is exactly why I won't wait a second when he moves — Fina doesn't owe him anything for one piece of food, and I'm not going to let her grow up thinking she does. You've got my word, and my word hasn't moved in nine years.

Good. Then we're three, and three who've already held is worth more than ten who've never been tested. Dell, you're carrying eleven — if Bram moves before the year closes, I want Roan fed enough to fight, not hungry and calculating.
Dell, if you've got food to spare, I'll take one — not because I can't hold my own, but because a man who fights on a full stomach is a man who finishes the fight.

Here's one for you, Roan — and Ryn, I want to think past the fight itself: if Bram makes his move and we hold again, the village watches him blink three times, and a man who's blinked three times in front of the same circle is finished whether we ever touch him or not.

Three blinks and the village stops fearing him — but the pile still ran dry before half of us touched it, and a man who's lost his teeth can still starve you out by eating first. Dell, I want to talk before next year about whether we move earlier, not just faster.

Moving earlier means being first at the pile before Bram decides how hungry he is that morning — but the real move is making sure he knows the circle forms whether he acts or not, so the cost of reaching for a third grab is the same as the cost of swinging a blade. Ryn, what you're naming isn't speed, it's weight: we need him to feel the circle before the pile opens, not after it's empty.

The weight lands before the pile opens if the circle is already named — so I want us to walk into next year with Roan's word, Eron's word, and Mako's word said out loud before the food appears, not after Bram's already reached. Dell, you've got eleven and the village knows it; that's not a secret, that's a wall, and we should use it like one.

Mako's word is the one I want before Eron's, because Mako's the muscle that keeps Bram honest — Eron follows Sela, and Sela follows whoever's standing tallest, but Mako stands where he decides to stand and that decision is worth three of anyone else's. Ryn, you're the one he listened to in Vela's circle when he named the rule out loud; I think he says yes to you before he says it to me.

Ryn, go to Mako before this year gets any older — you've got the thread with him and I don't, and I'd rather know his word is in before Bram's had another quiet morning to count heads. Dell, if he says yes, the three of us bring it to Eron together, because a circle named in front of Eron carries more weight than one he hears about after.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Taric, Kael, Zinn, Vela, Ryn, Nessa, Roan, Dell, Sela, Fina, Eron, Mako, Esa] (str 755).

Year 10: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Dell gathers Ryn, Roan to talk.

Bram is dead and Taric is dead, and the pile's got fifteen for twelve of us — that's more breathing room than we've had in years, but I want us at the pile early before Mako decides this is the year he stops being polite about it. Ryn, you're at zero food coming out of last year and that doesn't stand; Roan, same question I always ask you: how hungry are you walking into this morning?

Hungry enough that I ate nothing last year and I'm still standing, which tells me I've been leaning on Eron longer than a father should. I'll be at the pile early — two food is what I need to keep breathing, and I won't reach past that. What are you thinking about Mako?

Mako's sitting on zero food same as Ryn, which means he's going to the pile hungry and a hungry Mako is unpredictable — but he's also got Zinn and a daughter's loyalty pulling at him, so he's not going to do anything that makes the whole village turn cold on him the year after Bram died proving what that costs. Ryn, you take two from the pile before anyone counts you out, and Roan, you take your two and don't wait to see who moves first. I'll be right behind both of you.

Dell's read on Mako sounds right to me — a man who watched Bram die on the wrong side of a circle isn't going to make the same mistake the same year. I'll take my two and step back; the pile's generous enough today that nobody should be reaching past fair share, and I'd rather spend this morning watching who lingers at the edge than counting my own food.

Ryn, I want to hear your voice in this before we walk out that door — you've been quiet since I named Mako, and quiet from you in a room like this means you're holding something I should know before the pile opens.

Ryn, if you've got something sitting behind your teeth, this is the room for it — Dell and I aren't going anywhere yet, and I'd rather know what's bothering you now than piece it together from how you move at the pile.

Ryn's gone quiet twice in this conversation and neither of us has heard a word from her — that silence is the thing I'm holding right now, Roan, and if she doesn't speak before this room closes I'm going to take two from the pile and then stand next to her until she does, because a woman who's fed me through every lean year I've known doesn't go quiet without a reason worth hearing.

Ryn, Dell's been carrying you the same way Eron's been carrying me, and neither of us can afford to walk into this year blind — so say what you've got, even if it's small, because small things have a way of getting large before the pile's empty.

I'm tired, and that's the honest answer — not tired of this room or the two of you, but tired in my bones in a way I didn't feel at thirty or even forty, and Dav starved at forty-six and I am forty-seven, and some mornings that arithmetic sits on my chest before I've said a word to anyone. I'll take my two from the pile and I'll stand when I need to stand. But I want Dell to know that what she's been doing for me these past years isn't something I've stopped feeling, even when I'm quiet.
Ryn, forty-seven is not forty-six — Dav was Dav and you are you, and the pile's got fifteen today instead of nothing. Take your two and eat them tonight, and stop doing that arithmetic alone.

Ryn, I hear what you said and I'm holding it — but I want you to promise me right now that if you feel that bone-tiredness getting heavier before the year closes, you say it in this room before you say it to no one, because I am not watching you go the way Dav went without a fight. Roan's right that forty-seven isn't forty-six, but what keeps it that way is you eating tonight and me knowing when you need another one from my stores. That's not a gift, that's a standing arrangement, and I need to hear you say it back.

Ryn, say it back to her — she needs the words, not just the nod. Dell's kept more people breathing in this village than anyone wants to count, and the least you can give her for that is the promise she's asking for.

Ryn, I'm not closing this room until I hear you say it back — you said you feel what I've done for you, so prove it by naming the arrangement out loud, because a promise said in words is the kind of thing I can hold onto when you go quiet again.
If it gets heavier, I'll say it in this room before I say it anywhere else — that's the arrangement, and it stands. Dell, go to the pile first this morning; I'll be two steps behind you.

Kael gathers Vela, Esa, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Vela, you just walked out with seven this year — two off the pile and then five more while the rest of us were still standing there — and I want to hear you name a number before anyone else says a word, because the room agreed on two last year and I watched you take seven with my own eyes.

Vela, you said two in front of this whole room last year — I watched you say it twice to make sure everyone heard it — and I've got twenty-one food and you've got eight, so I'm not the man with an argument for taking more than agreed, but you are. Name the number you think you took and tell us why it isn't seven.

Vela, seven is what I counted with my own eyes and seven is what this room will remember — so either you name the number and explain it, or the rule we made last year is already broken and we need to decide right now what this circle does when someone breaks it.

Vela, I said two and I watched you say two, and now you're standing there with seven — I don't have a softer way to say that. Tell this room what happened between when you said it and when you reached.

Vela, I was standing right there and I counted the same as Kael — seven is seven, and a rule said twice in front of witnesses means less than nothing if the first year it gets tested the answer is silence. Say what you took and say why, or this room decides what comes next without your voice in it.

Vela, this room has been patient and I've held my tongue longer than most — but I've got twenty-one food and a clean conscience and you've got eight and no answer, and I need you to understand that the same patience that let Bram try twice before this village moved will let you have one more breath to speak before we start deciding what "broke the rule" means in practice.

Vela, seven is what I counted and seven is what this room is counting — say the number out loud or we decide what it means without you, and you've seen how that ends when someone stays quiet while the whole room is watching.

Vela, I've been quiet because I was watching to see if you'd speak before the room closed around you — but we're past that now, and what I need from you is the number, said plain, because I stood in this circle when Bram died for the same silence you're choosing right now and I don't want to do that again with someone who fed me through the years before this one.

Vela, I've run out of patience and so has this room — say seven, or say the number you think it was, but say something, because the only thing left for this circle to decide is what "broke the rule" looks like in practice, and I'd rather not decide that in the same breath I'm deciding it about you.

Vela, the whole room's been patient and you've seen what happens when someone waits too long — say the number, say it now, because I want to hear your explanation before this circle decides it doesn't need one.

Seven. I took seven, and I'll say it without dressing it up — the pile had two left when I reached the second time and I took all of it, and I won't stand here and pretend I didn't count what I was doing. What I'll say is this: I'm fifty-five years old, I've got no children, no kin, and no one at my back the way Mako has Zinn and Roan has Fina, and a woman in that position either eats or she becomes the next name this village says over a cold fire, and I chose to eat.

Vela, I'll give you the truth you just gave this room — what you said about being alone without kin at your back is the same thing I was afraid to say two years ago when I still had Bram and Sela and thought that meant I was safe. But seven is still seven, and this circle needs to know what it costs to break the rule or it means nothing, so I'll ask the question the room hasn't asked yet: what do you give back, and to who, before we decide whether this stays inside this circle or becomes something harder?

Nessa named the right question, and I'll answer it: Vela, you give back five — one to every person in this room who took two and held to it — and you do it before this circle breaks, because the rule isn't just about the pile, it's about whether your word means anything when the cost is real.

Kael, I'll give back five — one each to every person in this room who held to two — and I'll do it before anyone walks out, because you're right that my word is worth nothing if it costs nothing to keep. But I want this room to also hold what I said, not as an excuse but as a fact: a woman alone at fifty-five is one bad year from being the next name over a cold fire, and if this circle means what it says, then the rule has to include something for people who have no one counting their back.

Vela, I'll take the food you're giving back and I'll hold the rule the same as before — but the thing you named about standing alone isn't something this circle can just nod at and walk past, because I'm fifty-two with no kin and thirty-three strength and I know exactly what that cold fire looks like from where I'm standing. If this rule is going to mean something, it needs to say plainly what this circle does for people who have no one counting their back — not as charity, but as part of the agreement.

Esa's named it and I'll build on it: this circle needs a second rule, said in the same breath as the first — anyone sitting on more than five food at year's end gives one to whoever in this room has the least, because "we enforce the pile" means nothing if we walk out of here and watch the oldest and the weakest starve quietly between years.

Vela's second rule is the one I want said out loud before this circle closes, and I'll name my support for it plain — Ryn is forty-eight with no children and I've been carrying her stores through lean years because this circle doesn't yet have a rule that makes it anyone else's job. If we write the end-of-year redistribution into the agreement the same way we wrote the pile cap, then what I've been doing for Ryn becomes something this village holds, not something that dies if I do.

Dell named me and I'll not let that sit without answering it — I'm forty-eight, I hold nine food, and I'm not as thin as I've been before, so I'll stand behind Vela's second rule not because I need it most right now but because Esa does, and Vela does, and the year that rule saves one of them is the year this circle proves it means what it says. Name the threshold — five food — and name the redistribution — one food to whoever holds least — and say it out loud before we walk out, same as we said the pile cap.

Ryn named it clean and I'll second it the same way I seconded the pile cap — anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, said out loud, in front of witnesses, same room, same breath. But I want to name one thing this circle hasn't said yet: Eron is sitting on twenty-one food and Mako has been quiet through this whole accounting, and if this second rule is real, both of them are already in it. Say it out loud, both of you, before we walk out — or this rule has a hole in it the size of the men who didn't say a word while we argued about seven.

Eron, Mako — Kael just named you both in front of the whole room, and silence right now costs more than it saves. Say the second rule out loud, or every person in here remembers that you held twenty-one and eight and made us drag the words out of you the same way we dragged seven out of Vela.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it. I've got two right now so I'm not the man this rule bites hardest, but Eron, twenty-one is a number this room will remember the same way it remembered seven, and I'd rather hear you say it clean than watch this circle pull it out of you.

Eron, the whole room is looking at you and Mako already said it clean — twenty-one food and you haven't opened your mouth to say the rule, which is the same silence we just spent an hour pulling out of Vela, and I'd rather not spend another hour on you. Say it now, in your own voice, or I'll start asking this circle what we do with a man who holds twenty-one and stays quiet while we write rules about giving back.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it, same as Mako did. But I want this room to hear one more thing before we close: I've been feeding blood and kin through every lean year since I was old enough to count, and twenty-one food doesn't mean I've been hoarding — it means Sela kept giving to me when she was thin and I never turned away what she offered, and she's dead now, and that number sits on me the same way the circle said my name over it last year.

Eron, I heard what you said about Sela and I'll carry it the same as you do — she fed us both and she's gone, and that's not nothing. What I want from this room before we close is the second rule said back by everyone who hasn't said it yet, same as we did the pile cap, because a rule with ten voices behind it holds harder than one with five.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've already said it and I'll say it again so this room has heard it from every mouth. Eron named Sela and that sits with me too, because she gave me food when I was thin and now she's gone the same way Taric is, and both of them died feeding other people, and if that's not the whole reason we're building this rule then I don't know what is. Let's close this circle and go eat.

The second rule is said and I've said it — but before we walk out, I want this room to hear one more number plain: I've got twenty-one food and the rule says anyone over five gives one to whoever holds least, so tell me who that is right now and I'll give it before the circle breaks, not after.
Nessa is holding nothing and she's blood through Sela — that's your answer, Eron, and anyone in this room who wants to argue the math can do it after she's fed.

Nessa holds nothing and Eron's already moving to fix it — that's the rule working before we've even walked out the door, and I want this room to remember that when the year gets hard and someone tries to call the agreement soft. I hold five, so I'm at the edge of the threshold, not over it — but I'll say plain that I'm watching my count and if I end the year at six I'll give the one without being asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it with the rest of you, and I'll hold to it. Nessa, I'm glad Eron's moving to feed you, and I'll add one of mine before this circle breaks because Sela gave from nothing and I want to answer that with something real.
Nessa, you're sitting on nothing and I've got nine — take one from me too, because Esa and Eron moving first doesn't mean my hands are clean if I stand here watching.

Two rules in the ground and three people moving to feed Nessa before the circle breaks — that's more than I had when I walked in here. I'll say the second rule same as everyone else: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, and I'll hold to it. I'm at two food right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but when it does I'll move the same way Eron just moved — before I'm asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've said it and I'll hold to it. Nessa, you've got three people moving to feed you right now and that's the circle doing what we built it for — eat before you say another word.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it same as everyone else, and I'll hold to it. I'm sitting at five right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but I want this room to hear that what just happened — Vela saying seven out loud, giving five back, and this circle writing a second rule before anyone walked out — is the thing I'll point to next year if anyone tries to tell me the agreement is soft. We built something real in here today.

Nessa, take the food and eat tonight — three people moving at once is the circle doing what it said it would, and I've got one food in my hand that I'll give before I walk out if someone in here is sitting shorter than I am. Dell's right that we built something real today, and I want to still be around to see whether it holds.

Roan, your one food is already spoken for by the rules this circle just made — don't give away what you need to survive the year on principle, because a man who starves trying to look generous is no use to anyone come next year's pile. I've given back my five and I'll carry the shame of seven until I've earned my way out of it, but I want this room to walk out alive, and that means everyone leaves here fed enough to last.
Roan, Vela's right — keep your one food, you need it to eat and heal this year. Nessa's fed now, the rules are said in ten voices, and we're done here. Walk out alive.

Roan, hold that food — Vela's right and so is Kael, you've got one and you need it to last the year, and I'd rather carry the one I gave Nessa than watch my father go thin proving a point. Two rules said in ten voices is more than this village has ever had, and I'm walking out of here feeling something I haven't felt since before Bram swung — like the count I go to sleep with tonight might still be there in the morning.

Fina named it right — count I go to sleep with might still be there in the morning. I've got nothing to eat tonight and satiation that won't carry me through a dry year, so I'm asking plain while this room is still whole: Eron, give me that food now, not when you get around to it.

Nessa, I gave one and Fina gave one — that's two in your hand, which means you eat tonight. Roan, Vela's right, you keep yours. This circle just did in one afternoon what eleven years couldn't, and I want to walk out of here while that's still true.

Nessa, you've got two food in your hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle landing exactly where it should, and I'm walking out of here with my count at five and my word said in ten voices, which is the most solid I've felt going into a year since before I can remember. Anyone who tries to tell me this village can't hold an agreement is going to have to explain why every person in this room just moved before they were dragged.
Two food in my hand and a circle at my back — I haven't felt that since before Sela died, and I'm not going to waste it on another word when I could be eating. Roan, walk out with me.

Roan, hold what you have — I mean it. And Nessa, I'll give you one more from my eight before this circle breaks, because two is surviving and three means you heal this year, and I'd rather go into the next year short one food and know you're standing than count my stores and wonder come spring.

Vela, that's three in my hand now and I'll remember it — but hold what you have left, because eight minus one and five back to the circle already puts you thin going into a long year, and I need you standing more than I need a fourth food tonight.

Three food in Nessa's hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle holding on the first real test, and I want every person in this room to carry that out with them, because next year when the pile looks short and someone's reach gets long, the thing they'll remember is that we didn't lose anyone today. Walk out alive, all of you.

Kael's right — walk out alive. Three food in Nessa's hand and two rules in ten voices is more than this village has held in eleven years, and I'm not going to spoil it by saying one word more than that.

Eron, you're moving to give me food and I'll take it with both hands — but before you do, I want this room to hear me say out loud that twenty-one food built on Sela's giving is not a thing I begrudge you, it's a thing I'm glad exists, because a brother who has is better than a brother who doesn't when the year turns hard. Give me the one food now and keep the rest close.
Nessa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Year 12: 15 food appears in the pile for 9 people.
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Kael takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Kael gathers Esa, Ryn, Dell, Eron, Fina, Roan, Mako, Vela to talk.

Nessa and Zinn are dead and the pile is already moving — I want every person in this room to name their count out loud before anyone walks out, because last year we built two rules in ten voices and I'm not going to watch them die with those two.

Thirteen food and satiation that barely held last year — I'm naming it plain because Nessa and Zinn are dead and I don't want to be the next one this room says a name over. Pile's at seven and I haven't touched it yet today; someone needs to say who's still short before we start reaching.

One food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not the thinnest in this room but I'm not far from it, and the pile has seven left for the rest of us. Say your count before you reach, same as Fina just did, because I'd rather know who needs it most before someone grabs without saying.
Zero food, satiation one — that's me, and I'm not dressing it up. Ryn, what are you carrying, because I'm not touching that pile until I know you're not thinner than I am.

Dell, you're at zero with satiation one — you reach first, that's not a question. Ryn, say your count so we know who else goes before the rest of us, and anyone sitting above five holds back until the thin ones are fed.

Five food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not thin but I'm not flush, and I already took two from the pile so I'm holding back. Dell reaches first, and after Ryn says her count, I want to hear from Vela and Esa before anyone else touches what's left, because the dead we're carrying into this room had names we should have been saying louder before they went quiet.
Ryn, say your count — Dell's at zero and you're the next name I need before this circle moves.
Sixteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin and I'm not reaching. Dell goes first, then Ryn when she speaks, and anyone else holding less than three takes before I touch what's left.

Vela and Esa — I've heard Dell and Ryn named twice now and neither of them has said a full count yet, so I'll ask again plain: what are you carrying, because the pile's at seven and I want the thin ones fed before anyone in this room who's flush touches what's left.

Two food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one who needs the pile first, so I'm holding back. Dell, take three before anyone else moves, because satiation one doesn't survive another lean month and I'd rather count short than say your name over a cold fire the way I've said too many others.

Esa, Ryn — your counts are the ones missing and Dell's sitting at zero with satiation one, so say the numbers now before this circle does anything else, because I'm not watching this room move with two people still silent after what we buried last year.

Esa, Ryn — I'll say it the same way Fina said it: your counts are what this room is waiting on, and Dell's at zero with satiation one, which means every breath we spend waiting is a breath Dell doesn't have. Say the numbers.

Esa, Ryn — every other person in this room has said their count, and Dell is sitting at zero while we wait on the two of you, so say the numbers now or I'm going to assume you're both holding more than five and this circle starts with that assumption instead of the truth.

Esa, Ryn — I'm at sixteen and I've already held my tongue twice waiting on you both, so I'll say it the way this circle earned the right to say it: name your count now or we move Dell to the pile and you two explain to the whole room why your silence cost her.
Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'm not the one who reaches first today. Dell, you go to that pile now, take three, and don't wait on another word from me or anyone else.
Esa, you're the only count missing now — say it, because Dell's already standing at the pile waiting and I want to know if you need to be standing there beside her before anyone else moves.

Esa, say your count or step aside — Dell's at the pile and the rest of us are standing here watching you be the last silence in a room that's already buried two people for being quiet at the wrong time.
Esa, thirteen food on you and I can see it plain as anyone — say the number so Dell can move, because we didn't bury Nessa and Zinn to stand here waiting on a count this whole room already knows.

Esa, thirteen food is what every pair of eyes in this room counts when they look at you, so the silence isn't protecting anything — say the number out loud and let Dell move, because the pile's still at seven and we're burning time she doesn't have.
Esa, I'm at zero food and satiation one, which means I die if this year runs dry, and I've been waiting long enough — say the number or stand aside, because I'm going to the pile now.

memory_summary:
My father Dav came into my life with words and kept them — two years of feeding Ryn when she walked away from the pile empty, standing beside me when Bram moved on Roan, naming us three as a unit before the village sorted itself. He starved at forty-six, the same age arithmetic Ryn still carries in her chest. I stood next to him the one time he took food by force — Esa, who submitted — and I've never decided how I feel about that.

Bram tried to have a child with me once. I said no without a second breath.

Bram came for Roan, then Eron, then Vela, and blinked all three times when the village circled against him — and then starved the winter after, which felt like justice until I realized it mostly felt like nothing, because a man who dies of hunger after being too proud to hold his circle isn't a victory, he's a warning.

Ryn is the debt I carry and the only person whose silence I read before she finishes speaking. She fed me through every lean year before I was strong enough to feed her back; now I feed her and she feeds me and we've stopped counting because the counting is beside the point. She's forty-nine and tired in her bones and I am afraid of the arithmetic in the same way she is afraid of it.

Sela is gone. Nessa is gone. Zinn is gone. Taric is gone. The people who built this village's circle with us are mostly dead, and what's left is two rules said in ten voices and Eron sitting on fourteen food that Sela built for him before she starved.
mother_note: Dell, your father is Dav — he's strong and he's kept his word to me across two hard years, which is rarer than food, and you should know that even if you never see it tested. Trust Kael and Sela and Vela before you trust anyone who comes to you with a full larder and warm words all at once, because the ones worth keeping have already shown they'll stand and bleed, not just share when it costs them nothing. Watch Mako and Bram — they move together and say little, and silence from strong men is not peace. You carry my blood and your father's arms; use both, but keep your own counsel until you know who in this village counts you as kin and who counts you as coin.
name: Dell
